Hello again!

So it has become a running theme that I need to integrate a spatial filter into my setup. Will do. I really like the price I see for the SF-1T from Creative Stars [http://www.creativestars.com/](http://www.creativestars.com/)

But here's the thing - I am not exactly sure either what objective or what pinhole to go for. The only basis of comparison that I have is a 20X microscope objective that I have played with. I found this lens to expand my beam much larger than what I desire. So do I want 10X?

If so, then here's the numbers I have so far: 

Wavelength - 532nm

10X focal length - 16.25mm

Beam diameter - ? - this is where I get stumped. The spec sheet for my laser [http://www.lasermotion.com/TEXT/JDSU411 ... eet%20.gif](http://www.lasermotion.com/TEXT/JDSU4116TestSheet%20.gif) gives only waist diameter (0.6mm). What do I do? Do I need to calculate from beam divergence (1.2mrad) or something?

For just one fleeting moment, I thought it might be as simple as putting a fine ruler across my beam down where I will be placing said spatial filter, but if that number is to be believed, my beam is 5mm diameter at that point...!?

Arg.

Um, OK.. By the time my beam reaches the the point my spatial filter is to be inserted, it has been split once and travelled a total of 100 inches (254cm) from the laser head. Is it now necessary that I learn a bunch of math and figure out how much it has spread over that distance?

I have no idea how to do this. I found a nifty spatial filter calculator online [http://www.newport.com/OpticalAssistant ... nhole.aspx](http://www.newport.com/OpticalAssistant/SpatialFilterPinhole.aspx) and this wouldbe great but for the fact that I have no idea what my beam diameter is.

I beg you, I implore you, please help me figure out what I need to know in order to buy the right parts for my spatial filter...

posts.content_md: Get a 20x and 25 micron pinhole. After that; get a 40x, a 10x and then maybe a 10 micron pinhole if you really need it. When you've got those, get another spatial filter body (or two) cheap via ebay. You'll have the set for years, always use them, and be happy doing it because the beams are soooo clean.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: *sob*  *snuffle*  Please help me get a spatial filter going
posts.content_md:
I find I almost always use the 5x and 10x for the reference beams with large collimators and with no collimator, and occasionally the 20x if the collimator is small with a short FL.

If your not using a collimator yet, the a 5x would be the best choice if you can back the spatial filter up that far so as to get your desired illumination. The longer the fl of the lens the less diverging it will be. This will help you when you get a collimator so you not a mile from the collimator to get the conjugate (convering at same rate as the divergence of the original reference beam).

Remember, you want the beam diameter bigger then your plate so that you get a more even coverage of light. If your using a collimator that is about the size of the plate, then the light diameter should be a little bigger then the collimator.

posts.content_md:
> **Justin W:** If I understand correctly, I will want to find the point where said spatial filter has expanded my beam somewhat larger than my plate, and insert there a parabolic mirror that has a focal length of that very distance(?)... This parabolic mirror will reflect a collimated beam at that time, but.... seeing as how I do not want a collimated beam of light reflecting straight back to my spatial filter, I must cock the parabolic mirror at an angle, yes? Will this not result in coma or some other type of mis-concentration of the light?

You are correct on both points, but fortunately small errors in collimation and other minor optical aberrations are not at all noticeable in simple display holograms if the objects are not too far from the plate. When using a mirror collimator, you want to use a folded setup so that the angle between the expanding beam going to the mirror and the reflected beam to the plate is as small as possible. In this type of setup, often a black card or other light barrier is helpful in making sure that only the collimated light from the mirror hits the plate and object.
